meta.title: Who originally recorded "Sway"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dean Martin’s 1954 Capitol hit was a cover. Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta recorded it first, as the Mexican instrumental “¿Quién será?”, on RCA Victor in 1953.
meta.ogDescription: Not Dean Martin. Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta cut it first in 1953 for RCA Victor, as the Mexican bolero-mambo “¿Quién será?”.

answer.label: Not a Dean Martin original — a 1953 instrumental by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta on RCA Victor
answer.originalArtist: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta
answer.originalArtistDates: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz, 1915-2008 · Mexican bandleader, composer and orchestra leader
answer.sourceLine: Dean Martin’s 1954 Capitol single is so completely the version people carry around that the song reads as his invention. It isn’t. The song is a Mexican bolero-mambo called “¿Quién será?”, written by Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz, and Beltrán Ruiz recorded it first — as an instrumental cha-cha-chá for RCA Victor in 1953. Norman Gimbel’s English lyric, written the following year, is a different text on the same tune: it turned a wistful Spanish song into a dancefloor one, and the Spanish original quietly disappeared from the English-speaking record of the song.

trail: Wikipedia’s account of the song states that Pablo Beltrán y su Orquestra recorded the first version in 1953 as an instrumental cha-cha-chá ↗, and that Norman Gimbel wrote the English lyric the following year.
The bandleader’s own entry confirms the dates and the Mexican origin — Pablo Beltrán Ruiz, 1915-2008, composer and bandleader ↗, co-writer of the 1953 song and leader of the orchestra that cut it.

MusicBrainz carries the composition as a Spanish-language work credited to both writers — “¿Quién será?”, Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz ↗, with the later English recordings attached as performances of it.

UCLA’s Frontera archive holds an early Seeco 78 of “Quien Sera” by Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo ↗, catalogued as a bolero-mambo by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz — evidence of how fast the song moved through Latin dance bands before any English version existed.

authors.name: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta
authors.heading: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta
authors.metaLine: Mexican bandleader and composer, 1915-2008 · RCA Victor, 1953
authors.bio: Beltrán Ruiz led one of the busiest Mexican dance orchestras of the 1950s, working steadily in film as well as on record — he wrote music for pictures starring Pedro Infante, Tin Tan and Cantinflas. His orchestra cut “¿Quién será?” as an instrumental cha-cha-chá for RCA Victor in 1953, the first version of the song on record. He is also credited as its co-composer alongside Luis Demetrio, and that double role — writer and first performer — is exactly what got flattened once the English version took over.

authors.name: Dean Martin
authors.heading: Dean Martin
authors.metaLine: American singer and actor, 1917-1995 · Capitol Records, 1954
authors.bio: Martin recorded “Sway” for Capitol in 1954 with Dick Stabile’s orchestra, backed with “Money Burns a Hole in My Pocket.” It reached number 15 on the Billboard best-seller chart and number six in the UK, and his easy, half-amused delivery is the reason the song has never left circulation. Nothing about the record is a fault — it is simply a cover, made a year after the song was already on tape in Mexico.

authors.name: Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz (music and Spanish lyric); Norman Gimbel (English lyric)
authors.heading: The writers
authors.metaLine: Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz, 1953 · Norman Gimbel, English lyric, 1954
authors.bio: Luis Demetrio wrote the song with Pedro Infante in mind, and by his own account Beltrán Ruiz supplied only its opening musical material while Demetrio composed the rest and the Spanish lyric. Because Demetrio sold his rights to Beltrán Ruiz, the song has often been credited to Beltrán Ruiz alone. Norman Gimbel wrote an entirely new English lyric in 1954 under the title “Sway” — it is not a translation of the Spanish, which is why the two versions feel like different songs sharing a melody.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong origin story
misattribution.intro: “Sway” is treated in the English-speaking world as a Dean Martin invention. It is a Mexican song that already existed, under a different title, in a different language, with no lyric about swaying at all.

items.why: His Capitol single with Dick Stabile’s orchestra is the version that charted in the US and UK and the one every later cover answers to. Nothing on the record signals a Spanish-language source.

items.who: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta, RCA Victor, 1953.
items.why: They recorded “¿Quién será?” as an instrumental cha-cha-chá a year before Martin’s single. Being an instrumental, it left no lyric for English listeners to recognise it by.

items.who: Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz; Norman Gimbel wrote the separate English lyric.
items.why: Demetrio wrote the song for Pedro Infante and said Beltrán Ruiz contributed only its opening material — but Demetrio sold his rights to Beltrán Ruiz, so credit has often gone to Beltrán Ruiz alone. Gimbel’s 1954 English words are a new text, not a translation.

misattribution.truthLine: Dean Martin sang it second, in a language and with a lyric the song did not start out in.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The usual story of an eclipsed original is that a bigger star made a louder record. Here something sharper happened: the English version isn’t a translation. Norman Gimbel wrote a fresh lyric about dancing and attraction over a Mexican song whose Spanish words were melancholy and searching — and gave it a new title. Once a song is called “Sway” in English, there is nothing left in it pointing back to “¿Quién será?”, and no reason for an English-speaking listener to go looking.

The original also never had a chance to become the definitive version even in Spanish. Beltrán Ruiz’s 1953 record was an instrumental, so it carried no words to remember it by; Luis Demetrio had written the song for Pedro Infante, who sang it in a 1954 film and made it his own across Latin America. So the song split into three lives — an instrumental first take, an Infante standard in Spanish, and a Dean Martin hit in English — and only the last one travelled.
detailsBody: 1953 — Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta record “¿Quién será?” as an instrumental cha-cha-chá for RCA Victor. This is the first recording of the song.
1953-54 — the song circulates in Latin America as a bolero-mambo; La Sonora Matancera, with Nelson Pinedo singing, cut a vocal version for the Seeco label on 78rpm.
1954 — Pedro Infante, the singer Luis Demetrio originally wrote the song for, performs it in the film Escuela de vagabundos (School for Tramps); it becomes one of his signature songs.
1954 — Norman Gimbel writes an unrelated English lyric titled “Sway.” Dean Martin records it for Capitol with Dick Stabile’s orchestra; it reaches number 15 in the US and number six in the UK.
1999 and 2004 — Shaft’s “(Mucho Mambo) Sway” and Michael Bublé’s revival for 143/Reprise reintroduce the song to two more generations, both by way of the English lyric.
context.pull: It wasn’t translated. It was replaced.
